🐛 Bug
It seems if you export torch.flatten(x) where x.ndim == 1, torch.onnx exports a single Flatten op whose output is always 2D.
To Reproduce
class Flatten(torch.nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        return x.flatten()


x = torch.rand(100)
torch.onnx.export(Flatten(), x, 'flatten.onnx', opset_version=13)

print(Flatten()(x).shape)
print(onnx.load("flatten.onnx").graph.output[0])

You will see
torch.Size([100])
name: "1"
type {
  tensor_type {
    elem_type: 1
    shape {
      dim {
        dim_value: 1
      }
      dim {
        dim_value: 100
      }
    }
  }
}

which means torch expects 1D output but ONNX outputs 2D.
I think this condition is wrong. For 1D tensor with default parameters, dim=1, start_dim=0, and end_dim=-1. This condition becomes unexpectedly True as end_dim == dim - 2. I think we should skip this if end_dim is negative, or normalize negative end_dim.
Expected behavior
Flatten should not be used when the result will be 1D tensor. The exporter should call sym_help._flatten_helper.

🚀 Feature
We currently allow COO to CSR conversion via to_sparse_csr, but not CSR to COO.
>>> indices = tensor([[0, 0, 1, 1, 2], [1, 2, 0, 2, 2]])
>>> values  = tensor([1., 2., 0, 3., 4])
>>> s = torch.sparse_coo_tensor(indices, values, (3, 3))
>>> s.to_sparse_csr().to_sparse()
[...]
NotImplementedError: Could not run 'aten::to_sparse' with arguments from the 'SparseCsrCPU' backend. 

Motivation
A user might want to switch between these layouts to take advantage of their unique performance properties.
Pitch
We support COO to CSR conversion, let's support CSR to COO too.
Alternatives
The user could use the constructors, which would require a manual conversion of the index formats and doesn't have autograd support. Alternatively they could convert via the dense layout, but might not want to use the additional memory this requires. Further, the information of which zeros are specified or unspecified is lost via to_dense, which matters for operations such as torch.sparse.softmax.
>>> s
tensor(indices=tensor([[0, 0, 1, 1, 2],
                       [1, 2, 0, 2, 2]]),
       values=tensor([1., 2., 0., 3., 4.]),
       size=(3, 3), nnz=5, layout=torch.sparse_coo)

                       [1, 2, 2, 2]]),

>>> x = torch.ones(1,5,5)
>>> x
torch.Size([1, 5, 5])
>>> x.shape
torch.Size([1, 5, 5])
>>> x.data
tensor([[[0.7200, 0.5811, 0.7329, 0.8614, 0.3746],
         [0.5929, 0.1970, 0.7099, 0.8618, 0.1981],
         [0.5709, 0.3217, 0.0588, 0.6208, 0.1363],
         [0.6375, 0.2657, 0.2176, 0.8552, 0.1189],
         [0.2587, 0.1059, 0.6994, 0.1862, 0.2905]]])
Motivation
This may be a extremely controversial but I find that I often more interested on the shape of tensors, than the actual values.
Considering this, it seems justified to ask why the default repr for tensors could be changed to printing the shape. This would save time typing .shape? Perhaps  an alternative would be showing the shape of the tensor alongside the values:
>>> x = torch.ones(1,5)
>>> x
torch.Size([1, 5])
>>> x.shape
torch.Size([1, 5])
>>> x.data
tensor[1,5]([[0.7200, 0.5811, 0.7329, 0.8614, 0.3746]])
Reasons for not doing it:

What I'm asking is almost equivalent to suggesting that when you print a float in python you'd be given the decimal precision instead of the value
You want to follow numpy outputs as much as possible
Some packages may rely on the output being a certain format and therefore changing it would not be backward compatible

I'd be really interested in what other people think about this.

🚀 Feature
Avoid converting Tensors to Scalars for ops that have Tensor variance
Motivation
PyTorch has many ops that have both Scalar and Tensor variations. Sometimes, the overload is selected that converts a Tensor to Scalar, which causes a Tensor value from a backend device to be fetched onto the host for getting the Scalar argument.
This causes a bubble in execution (if we create lazy execution graphs, then these cause the graph to break as well). It would be good to allow ops to work on Tensor arguments, so that the ops can continue to work on tensors that are already in the backend device.
Pitch
As per the order of overloads, Tensor overloads come first, before Scalar overloads. However, in case of the optional arguments like Scalar? and Tensor? variations (example: clamp), the order is not determined similarly. The optional argument ordering should also be similarly handled (#67429)
Along with that, PyTorch also has an internal list of ops which allow converting numbers to Tensors. If more ops are allowed to convert numbers to Tensors, then it would reduce the number of cases Tensor values need to be sent to host. (#67435)
Example:



import torch
a = torch.Tensor(2, 3)
b = torch.Tensor(3)
c = a.clamp(0, b[0] - 1)  <- Here, clamp favors the Scalar? overload and gets the b[0] to host as a scalar value. Instead, it should be possible to send both the arguments as Tensors so that the execution continues to be on device.

nodes.bodyText:
Since the release of Ampere GPUs, pytorch has been using tf32 by default.  It is providing much better performance at the expense of somewhat lower accuracy. Nvidia has conducted a lot of experiments proving that convergence behavior of a wide variety of networks does not change when tf32 is used instead of regular fp32.
However, since pytorch is used not only for deep learning workloads, or for some non-standard deep learning workloads, the use of tf32 for matrix multiplication has resulted in a lot of confusion and sometimes bad results.
Going forward, we have a few options

Do nothing. Pros: most users get speedups, cons: issues and confusion will continue
Leave the default as is, but add warning to the first call using tf32, explicit setting of allow_tf32 would silence this warning (proposed here. Pros - results will no longer be a surprise, and users will be able to get the expected results without resorting to documentation. Cons - pytorch doesn't warn for normal operations, so this would create bad precedent
Use tf32 in nn layers (linear, rnn etc), but disallow it for raw matmul operations (proposed here. Pros - networks using nn operations will get speed up while people experimenting with pure matmul operations will still get exact results. Cons - it is really confusing when linear layer that calls matmul under the hood produces different results than matmul call. Also, if someone defines a network using matmuls and not nn.Linear or nn.linear they won't see the speed-up.
Disable tf32 matmul by default, possibly with the warning that it can be enabled. Pros - no surprise, accurate results. Cons - users who are getting speed-ups currently will have to manually enable tf32, or see reduced performance. If there's a warning, same con as option 2).
In my conversations with power users, they lean towards option 4), we should use this issue to find an acceptable solution.
cc @zasdfgbnm @ptrblck @CrisHY1995, @ssnl, @stas00, @t-vi, @ptrblck, @csarofeen, @zasdfgbnm, @wjablonski-work, please copy anyone else who is interested in this discussion.

🐛 Bug
The c10/util/variant.h file has been modified to be vendored inside the c10 namespace, which is great.  Moreover, the
inclusion guard at the top of the file has been renamed from MPARK_VARIANT_HPP to C10_UTIL_VARIANT_H_.  However,
c10/util/variant.h is the concatenation of several header files from this library, and so further down in c10/util/variant.h are
other inclusion guards like MPARK_LIB_HPP, MPARK_CONFIG_HPP, and so forth that remain.
This causes build errors when the same C++ source file includes torch/torch.h (or anything else that includes c10/util/variant.h),
along with other third party libraries that happen to also use this library from github.com/mpark/variant.
Additional context
I think the fix is just to rename the other inclusion guards to have names like C10_MPARK_LIB_H_ instead of MPARK_LIB_HPP, etc.
cc @malfet @seemethere
